```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
example_file <- function(name) system.file("examples", name, package = "spacescans")
```

spacescans links time-referenced geolocation data to the spatial and
contextual exposome. Its input is a cohort of location episodes: a
participant, a location (longitude and latitude) and the first and last day
spent there. For every location episode it computes area- or
buffer-weighted exposures such as the Neighborhood Deprivation Index,
walkability, noise, night-time lights or air pollution, or the distance to
the nearest feature, and by default it returns one row per participant.

The R package is a client of the spacescans Python pipeline. Every call
starts `python -m spacescans.bridge` in a separate process and exchanges
JSON files and Parquet tables with it, so a crash or Ctrl-C in Python never
takes your R session down. The code below does not run when this vignette
is built, because it needs the Python environment and the exposure data;
the two example scripts it shows are installed with the package and run by
the package's live tests.

## 1. Install the Python side once

```{r}
library(spacescans)
ss_install()          # a private Python 3.12 environment, built with uv
ss_doctor()           # interpreter, versions, extras, folders, disk, data
```

`ss_install()` puts the environment under
`tools::R_user_dir("spacescans", "data")` and never touches the Python on
your `PATH`. TEMIS needs one more extra: `ss_install(extras = "hdf4")`. If
your IT department provides an interpreter, point the package at it with
`ss_use_python()` or the `SPACESCANS_PYTHON` environment variable. The
supported platform is macOS 14 or later on Apple silicon.

## 2. Choose a data directory and get the data

No exposure data ships with spacescans. The catalog says where each dataset
comes from, and `ss_fetch()` downloads what you need from the providers or
from the project mirror, where the providers' terms allow it.

```{r}
ss_data_dir("~/ss-data")              # or set SPACESCANS_DATA_DIR
ss_catalog()                          # the variables, years, data and extras
ss_data_status("noise")
ss_fetch("noise", dry_run = TRUE)     # what would be downloaded (about 1.2 GB)
ss_fetch("noise")                     # resumable; shared files only once
```

Some provider datasets (for example EPA FAQSD) require you to accept their
terms. Read them with `ss_data_terms("faqsd")`; an interactive session asks
you, a script passes `accept_terms =`. Keep the data directory on a local
disk: spacescans warns when it, the cache or a run directory is inside
iCloud Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox or Box.

## 3. A minimal example

Three synthetic participants and the NPS noise model (Mennitt et al.), the
catalog source whose files are all on the project mirror. The script is
installed with the package:
`source(system.file("examples", "minimal-example.R", package = "spacescans"))`.

```{r, file = example_file("minimal-example.R")}
```

`res` has one row per participant (`P1`, `P2`, `P3`) and the columns `pid`,
`l50dba_exi`, `l50dba_imp` and `l50dba_nat`; `episodes` is the cohort with
the same three columns added, one row per location episode. The last line
checks the participant-level rule on P2, who has two location episodes.

## 4. Output levels

`ss_link()` returns one row per participant unless you ask for
`output_level = "episode"`. For participant *i* and variable *v* the value
is the mean of the participant's episode values weighted by contributing
days:

$$\bar{x}_{iv} = \frac{\sum_{e \in E_i} \sum_{t \in T_{ev}} d_{et}\, z_{etv}}{\sum_{e \in E_i} \sum_{t \in T_{ev}} d_{et}}$$

where $E_i$ are the participant's location episodes, $z_{etv}$ is the
spatial estimate (a buffer-weighted mean, or the distance to the nearest
feature) for episode $e$ in source period $t$ (a year, two weeks or a day),
$T_{ev}$ are the source periods that overlap the episode and have an
estimate, and $d_{et}$ is the number of days of that overlap, first and last
day included. A time-invariant source counts every day of the episode. Days
are counted per variable, so a participant can have a value for one variable
and not for another; a participant with no contributing day is kept, with a
missing value. Where two location episodes of one participant overlap in
time, each contributes its own days, so a calendar day both cover counts once
for each location. Variables derived after aggregation (the FARA flags, the
ACAG `_nbm` columns) are derived from the participant's means; see
`?ss_link`.

| | `"participant"` (default) | `"episode"` |
|---|---|---|
| rows | one per participant, in order of first appearance | one per location episode, in your order |
| columns | `pid` (your id's type) and the exposures | your columns, unchanged, and the exposures |
| `attr(res, "coverage")` | share of participants with a value | share of episodes with a value |

Both carry `attr(res, "features")` (what each column means),
`attr(res, "provenance")` (versions, code fingerprint, data receipts, cache
keys; no cohort values) and `attr(res, "output_level")`. `ss_coverage()`
estimates before a run how many location episodes fall inside each
variable's years and region; it counts episodes at either level, because it
looks only at dates and locations.

## 5. Link your cohort

A cohort has one row per location episode with the columns `pid`,
`startDate`, `endDate`, `longitude` and `latitude`. Other names can be
mapped with `cols`, and `PATID` is accepted for `pid`.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
cohort <- data.frame(
  participant_id = c("A", "A", "B"),
  start = as.Date(c("2015-01-01", "2017-06-01", "2016-03-15")),
  end = as.Date(c("2017-05-31", "2019-12-31", "2019-12-31")),
  lon = c(-86.158, -86.131, -85.680),
  lat = c(39.768, 39.790, 40.193),
  age = c(54L, 56L, 71L)
)
cohort
```

```{r}
cols <- c(pid = "participant_id", startDate = "start", endDate = "end",
          longitude = "lon", latitude = "lat")
ss_coverage(cohort, c("ndi", "walkability"), cols = cols)

res <- ss_link(cohort, c("ndi", "walkability"), cols = cols)
res                       # pid, ndi, NatWalkInd: one row for A, one for B
ep <- ss_link(cohort, c("ndi", "walkability"), cols = cols, output_level = "episode")
ep                        # your columns, unchanged, plus ndi and NatWalkInd
```

What `ss_link()` does, in order:

1. checks the cohort in R and reports problems by row number, never by
   value;
2. writes only the five required columns to a private run directory (mode
   0700, under `tools::R_user_dir("spacescans", "cache")/runs`); `age` and
   any other column never leave R;
3. checks that the data and the Python extras are in place, and otherwise
   tells you the exact `ss_fetch()` or `ss_install()` call to run;
4. runs the pipeline, showing progress; Ctrl-C stops it cleanly;
5. returns the participant table, or joins the exposures back onto your
   data frame by row (keeping its types and attributes), and warns when a
   variable has a value for fewer than 90% of the rows;
6. deletes the run directory (unless `keep = TRUE`). Should R be killed
   before it can, the next session's package load (or `ss_doctor()`,
   `ss_cache_clear()`) deletes it, since it holds the five cohort columns.

The C3 weights (which units each buffer around a location overlaps) are
cached under `tools::R_user_dir("spacescans", "cache")`, so linking the
same cohort again is fast. They can reveal where people were: see
`ss_cache_info()` and clear them with `ss_cache_clear()` when a project
ends.

## 6. Long runs as background jobs

```{r}
job <- ss_link(cohort, c("ndi", "noise", "vnl"), cols = cols,
               wait = FALSE, run_dir = "~/ss-runs/noise-vnl")
ss_job_status(job)
res <- ss_job_result(job)          # waits, builds the result as above, removes the run directory
```

`ss_job_result()` removes the run directory once it has the result (pass
`keep = TRUE` to `ss_link()` to keep it). A job started with an explicit
`run_dir` keeps running when R exits; in a new R session, instead of the
`ss_job_result()` call above, find it again from its run directory:

```{r}
job <- ss_job_attach("~/ss-runs/noise-vnl", cohort = cohort, cols = cols)
ss_job_status(job)
res <- ss_job_result(job)          # or ss_job_cancel(job) to stop it
```

## 7. Your own data

Register a dataset once and link it by name in later sessions, like a
catalog variable. Registration checks and prepares the files and stores
them, with a record of their metadata, in a registry directory (see
`?ss_datasets`); your original files are no longer needed by the link. A
dataset is a table keyed by a Census geography (static, yearly or daily),
GeoTIFF rasters (static, yearly, biweekly or daily, on one grid), or point,
line or polygon features, whose variable is the distance to the nearest
feature. This example needs no catalog data:

```{r, file = example_file("registered-dataset.R")}
```

`ss_datasets()` lists what is registered, `ss_dataset()` shows one record,
`ss_update_dataset()` changes its name, metadata or variable units,
`ss_remove_dataset()` deletes one, and `ss_link(custom = )` takes names,
ids or records, alone or with catalog variables. A table names its Census
geography in `key`, with the key column when it is not called `GEOID10`,
`GEOID` or the like:

```{r}
svi <- ss_register_dataset("~/data/svi_2020_tract.csv", name = "SVI 2020",
                           kind = "polygon_table", temporal = "static",
                           key = list(boundary = "tract", column = "FIPS"),
                           variables = data.frame(name = "RPL_THEMES", unit = "percentile",
                                                  description = "Overall SVI percentile"),
                           source = "CDC/ATSDR SVI 2020", version = "2020")
res <- ss_link(cohort, "ndi", custom = "SVI 2020", cols = cols)

# Rasters: one GeoTIFF per period; the period comes from the file name or `periods`.
pm <- ss_register_dataset(c("pm_2016a.tif", "pm_2016b.tif"), name = "PM2.5 biweekly",
                          kind = "raster", temporal = "biweekly",
                          periods = as.Date(c("2016-01-01", "2016-01-15")))
```

For a one-off dataset that you do not want to register,
`ss_custom_polygon()` (a CSV keyed by a Census geography, static or yearly)
and `ss_custom_raster()` (GeoTIFFs, one or one per year) build a definition
that points at your files where they are:

```{r}
own <- ss_custom_polygon("svi_tract.csv", boundary = "Tract", key_col = "FIPS",
                         value_cols = "RPL_THEMES", name = "CDC SVI")
res <- ss_link(cohort, "ndi", custom = own, cols = cols)
```

## 8. When something goes wrong

Every error inherits from `spacescans_error` and has a class for its kind,
so a script can react to exactly what it expects:

```{r}
res <- tryCatch(
  ss_link(cohort, "faqsd", cols = cols),
  spacescans_error_data_missing = function(e) {
    message(conditionMessage(e))    # includes the ss_fetch() call to run
    NULL
  }
)
```

See `?"spacescans-conditions"` for the list. For one pipeline config of your
own (the lower-level interface), see `ss_run()`, `ss_templates()` and
`ss_validate()`.
